concepts_addressed: The Execution Gap: Knowledge Without Action

frameworks.name: Promote-Convert-Deliver Loop
frameworks.definition: A simple three-function business loop for sub-$1M businesses: (1) Promote — let people know about the offer via paid ads and content; (2) Convert — an automated or semi-automated page or sales motion; (3) Deliver — a fixed back-end delivery cadence (e.g., one call per week). The only high-leverage variable input is the promotion layer.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that scattered information-seeking behavior — consuming news, courses, and expert opinions across domains — is driven by fear of being left behind rather than genuine strategic need; the fear is that ignoring a trend (AI, crypto, new tools) will cause obsolescence.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Fear of being left behind drives compulsive consumption; each new technology feels existential, so the entrepreneur abandons current focus to investigate, permanently fragmenting attention.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that for entrepreneurs below roughly $1M in revenue, the entire business reduces to three activities: letting people know about the offer (promotion), an automated or human-assisted conversion step, and delivering the product — and that the only high-variance, high-leverage input is promotion volume.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.speaker_term: inputs and outputs of the system
conditions: Offer with an existing conversion mechanism (automated page or sales call)
bounded_by: Businesses with large teams requiring coordination overhead
Businesses without a working conversion mechanism

claims.text: Alex Hormozi recommends that founders below $1M in revenue allocate roughly equal thirds of their working day to promoting (paid ads and content), building (improving the offer or delivery assets), and delivering the product — using a timer to enforce the split.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: No large team requiring significant management overhead
bounded_by: Businesses with large teams that create unavoidable managerial overhead

claims.text: Alex Hormozi states that focus is defined as doing one thing, which means any additional activity reduces focus by definition; entrepreneurs frequently introduce distractions they treat as necessary while remaining unaware that those activities are reducing their output.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
bounded_by: Biological necessities (sleep, food) represent unavoidable focus reduction

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that once a business action is working, the founder should continue repeating it without modification until it stops working — because fear that an action will stop working is distinct from evidence that it has stopped working.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Action has produced measurable positive results
claims.mechanism: Stopping a working action is driven by fear of future failure rather than evidence of current failure; this substitutes imagination for data.
bounded_by: Action must continue producing results; evidence of actual decline is a legitimate stopping signal

claims.text: Alex Hormozi delivered the identical sales presentation on day two of his book launch — same content, same structure — and generated approximately $25 million in sales on day two, with a significant portion from attendees who had watched day one, demonstrating that repetition of a working pitch is not limited by audience familiarity.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Live event context with re-attending audience
Book launch with prior day revenue established
claims.mechanism: Audiences re-watch content they trust; repetition compounds rather than fatigues demand for high-quality pitches.

numbers.axis: Day-two sales revenue from identical repeated presentation

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that entrepreneurs who consume large volumes of third-party information (books, courses, expert opinions) before they have an active business are operating rationally — they lack first-party data to test against, so external information is the only available signal; but once they have a working business, third-party consumption becomes mostly noise.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Applies to the transition from pre-business to active-business stages
claims.mechanism: First-party data (results from your own tests) is both more accurate and more directly applicable than third-party data (others' reported experiences); once first-party data exists, third-party data is redundant unless it addresses an active unsolved problem.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi states that the appropriate pattern for consuming information after having a working business is problem-driven rather than exploratory: identify a specific constraint (e.g., conversion rate dropping), seek targeted information on that constraint, implement the resulting ideas, and only then seek additional information.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.speaker_term: consume a YouTube video about conversion rates
conditions: Entrepreneur has an active working business with measurable outputs
claims.mechanism: Consuming information before exhausting current implementation options creates cognitive overhead without feedback; you cannot learn from data you have not yet gathered.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi warns against changing business tactics mid-experiment — specifically changing an offer, price, or page while a split test or structural change is still in progress — because premature intervention invalidates the current test and provides no data from either version.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.speaker_term: don't change things when a solution is on the way
claims.topic: The Execution Gap: Knowledge Without Action
conditions: A split test, price test, or structural change is currently running
claims.mechanism: Interrupting a mid-flight test discards the accumulated data and restarts the learning cycle; the sunk time yields no feedback and the new change generates no clean baseline.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that for most content and paid-ad businesses, the highest-leverage improvement lever is earlier in the funnel — ad click-through rate (CTR) — not the landing page; doubling CTR doubles the entire business, whereas page conversion improvements rarely exceed 10-20%.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.speaker_term: leverage in the creative is so much more powerful than the leverage on the page
conditions: Business relying on paid ads as primary traffic source
Landing page is already functional (not broken)
claims.mechanism: CTR improvements compound with CPM changes — a high-quality creative can simultaneously double CTR and compress CPM sixfold, creating an 18x total improvement — while page optimization cannot generate equivalent multiplicative gains.

numbers.axis: Potential improvement multiplier by funnel position

anchors.region: Combined ad CTR + CPM improvement (best-case creative)

bounded_by: If landing page is broken (e.g., converting at <1%), page fixes take priority
Price changes can also produce large late-funnel multipliers

claims.text: Alex Hormozi describes a cowboy testing method used internally at School.com: change the element, watch the metric, and keep or revert based on directional movement — without a formal A/B test — for lower-sensitivity decisions; reserve formal A/B testing for high-sensitivity decisions only.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Metric is directionally readable from change (not noise-dominated)
Traffic volume is sufficient to detect a meaningful signal within one week
bounded_by: High-sensitivity decisions (e.g., core pricing page) require proper A/B test setup
Insufficient traffic makes cowboy testing misleading — minimum roughly one week of traffic needed

claims.text: Alex Hormozi reports that School.com ran 16 formal A/B tests on its sign-up page and 14 of them lost, meaning the control outperformed every challenger; the sign-up page proved extremely difficult to improve even with high traffic volume, whereas ad creative variation routinely yielded 5x performance improvement.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.speaker_term: we've run 16 A/B tests, 14 of them lost
conditions: School.com sign-up page (high-traffic SaaS product page)
Ad creative tested on Meta platform
claims.mechanism: A page that has been iterated over time tends toward a local optimum that is hard to improve; ad creative explores a wider search space with more degrees of freedom.

numbers.axis: A/B test win rate by funnel element type

claims.text: Alex Hormozi observes that adding a third pricing tier (VIP at $249/year) to School.com's two-tier offering (monthly at $9, premium at $77/year) caused premium conversion rate to drop from approximately 20% to 5%, because the new high-anchor tier confused rather than elevated the middle tier in this context.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.speaker_term: our conversion to early rate was like 20% and then ... dropped to 5%
conditions: SaaS subscription product with three price tiers
Audience already primed to the two-tier structure
claims.mechanism: A third tier can dilute rather than anchor the middle tier when the price gap is too large relative to perceived value differentiation, causing buyer paralysis.

numbers.axis: Premium tier conversion rate as number of tiers changes

bounded_by: Does not apply universally; high-anchor third tiers do lift conversion in other pricing contexts

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that strategy is fundamentally the prioritization of scarce resources across competing options; for most early-stage entrepreneurs, there is insufficient data to make reliable prioritization decisions, and the correct response is to execute more before prioritizing.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.topic: The Execution Gap: Knowledge Without Action
conditions: Early-stage business with insufficient data history
claims.mechanism: Without a data baseline, prioritization is guesswork; volume of execution generates the data required to prioritize rationally.
bounded_by: At sufficient scale (e.g., School.com level), strategy and prioritization become the primary leverage

examples.text: Alex Hormozi describes his book launch day two: he gave the exact same sales presentation he had delivered on day one, unchanged. The team was told that conventional wisdom requires a different pitch on day two. Hormozi disagreed, arguing that if the presentation worked, repeating it would produce more sales because the act of asking again is what drives conversion — not novelty. The result was approximately $25 million in sales on day two, with many of the same attendees from day one re-purchasing or purchasing for the first time after watching the same content twice.

A member (identified as working with School.com) reports that their premium conversion rate was approximately 20% when selling two tiers (monthly $9 and annual $77 premium). When they added a VIP tier at $249 per year to raise average revenue per user, the premium conversion rate dropped to 5%. Hormozi comments that this is first-party data — the outcome is clear regardless of what general anchor pricing theory predicts.

Hormozi recounts how School.com attempted to improve its sign-up page over many iterations using formal A/B tests. Of 16 tests run, 14 produced results worse than the control. Despite very high traffic volume, the page resisted improvement. By contrast, when the team tested a different ad creative on Meta, it sometimes outperformed the previous creative by 5x. This asymmetry between page and creative leverage led Hormozi to conclude that ad creative volume is where he concentrates improvement effort.

A guest speaker in the session describes their own transition: in their earlier career, when they had no active business, they read many books, took courses, and consumed broadly. Once they had a working business, they largely stopped reading books — they report not having read one in approximately two years. Hormozi endorses this pattern: early-stage exploratory consumption is rational when first-party data is absent; once the business is running, seeking information only in response to specific observed problems is more effective than general consumption.

practices.text: When building a business below $1M in revenue, spend the first four hours of the day promoting (content and paid ads), the next four hours building (product, delivery assets), and the last portion delivering the product. Set a timer and enforce the split.
When a split test or price test is mid-flight, do not change any other element of the business until the test completes and you have read the data.
practices.topic: The Execution Gap: Knowledge Without Action

practices.text: Before running a formal A/B test, check whether your traffic volume is high enough to produce a statistically meaningful result within one week. If not, make a directional change and observe the metric — do not run underpowered tests.
Prioritize increasing ad creative volume and CTR over page conversion optimization; the multiplicative leverage from earlier-funnel improvements compounds across CPM, CTR, and downstream conversion.

Use problem-driven information consumption: identify a specific bottleneck in your business, find targeted content on that bottleneck, implement the top ideas, exhaust those ideas through testing, and only then seek more information.
Trust your existing framework when a significant external trend appears; only update your model when the trend demonstrably affects your first-party business metrics.
